blocks.title: Introduction to the Numeracy Facilitator Guide

content.text: Directorate of In-Service Training and Lifelong Learning (DITaLL-MoBSE)with the support of Learning Masterminds(LM) and Effective Intervention(EI) has developed this Facilitator Guide to support the preparation of in-service early years’ teachers to implement the foundational numeracy curriculum. In-service teacher preparation approaches will include training workshops, seminars and classroom support to ensure that teachers develop conceptual understanding of the contents and general learning-teaching approaches at the lower basic level. The Facilitator Guide has been developed to be used by teacher educators who will be facilitating the in-service education and training of various categories of teachers at the school level - classroom teachers, senior teachers, head teachers, coaches and cluster monitors for the implementation of the numeracy curriculum.

The Facilitator Guide covers key areas. The first exposes teachers to the CBC concept and a Professional Learning Community (PLC) initiative. The remaining key areas have a special focus on pedagogy and assessment, i.e., inclusive, creative learner-centred pedagogies and assessment for learning strategies that are required for improving learning outcomes in Gambian schools. The guide is designed to facilitate the education and training of teachers in urban, peri-urban and rural settings across the country.

The Facilitator Guide is arranged in sessions. Each session has a catalogue of activities for both participants and facilitators. These are carefully packaged to help the teacher ─ who is the focus of the implementation of the revised curriculum ─ to follow the sequence and progression of learning areas in the curriculum. It is to enable teachers to understand the content of the curriculum and related lesson planning; identification and use of resources, inclusive, creative learning-centred pedagogic approaches and assessment strategies.

Also captured in the guide is the plan for the initial national training to include the education and training of trainers at national, regional and school level teachers in the numeracy curriculum so that they are better positioned to begin the implementation throughout the country. The training involves the training of National Core Trainers, Regional Trainers and training of school level teachers across the country. This initial training shall be followed by regular in-service education and training (INSET) at both the school, cluster and regional levels as part of MoBSE’s PLC initiative to ensure school level teachers regularly engage in time-tabled continuous professional development sessions.
provide facilitators with the necessary tools and guidelines for training teachers for the effective implementation of the numeracy curriculum;
enable facilitators to understand the numeracy curriculum and its importance in the education, growth and development of the Gambian learners for national development;
provide guidelines to experts who are directly or indirectly involved in activities aimed at improving the quality of education in The Gambia.
should read thoroughly every activity captured under the various sessions to ensure that they have a conceptual understanding and imbedded meaning of each activity
should consult INSET Unit of DITaLL for any clarification and support
should ensure that the recommended training resources are available in their right quantities
should ensure that the approaches suggested for an effective delivery of the training are not exhaustive
should encourage the use of other creative strategies that can help achieve the goals of the training
As a guide, all participants in the various nationwide education and training programs and in the implementation of the curriculum should daily ask the following critical questions:
what do my participants need to know, understand, and be able to do? (Plan)
how do I teach effectively to ensure participants are learning? (Do)
how do I know participants are learning? (Reflect)
what do I do when some participants are not learning or others are not learning as expected? (Revise)
Users of this guide (facilitators), should therefore consider among other things:
what teachers must know, understand and be able to do,
what evidence demonstrates teaching effectiveness, and
what steps can be taken to continuously improve and build upon effective classroom instruction.

The Facilitator Guide is laid out in three columns labeled time/duration, activity, materials or resources needed. The resources or materials needed column provides a link to textual materials in the Facilitator Guide, Resource Packet, Teacher’s Guide and Pupil’s Book.
The training is designed to Support trainers and teachers to:

Understand the rationale for curriculum reform in The Gambia and appreciate the shift from a content-based curriculum to the Competency-Based Curriculum Framework (CBC/CBF), including its importance in preparing learners for the demands of the 21st century.
Understand learning gaps in The Gambian Numeracy Curriculum (GNC) and examine the curriculum changes introduced, including content, pedagogy, and cross-curricular competencies.
Recognize the importance of numeracy in developing foundational learning competencies, broader life skills, and lifelong learning.
Understand how numeracy concepts develop progressively within and across grades and apply this understanding to improve lesson delivery, learner support, and developmental appropriateness.
Examine and effectively use the Pupil Book and Teacher Guide to support preparation, lesson delivery, and implementation of the Gambian Numeracy Curriculum.
Identify and apply the key components and structure of the Teacher’s Guide and appreciate its role in supporting effective teaching and learning.

Demonstrate understanding and application of inclusive, equitable, creative, and learner-centred pedagogies, including strategies that promote active learner participation, learner independence, and mathematical fluency.
Understand barriers to learning, particularly those related to gender, inclusion, and Social and Emotional Learning (SEL), and apply strategies to address these barriers within numeracy instruction.
Apply explicit instruction approaches and practical strategies for teaching foundational numeracy concepts, including:
Use concrete, pictorial, and abstract/symbolic approaches (CPA) to support learners’ progression from hands-on experiences to abstract numerical understanding.
Engage in demonstration lessons and microteaching activities to strengthen practical classroom skills required for effective implementation of the GNC.
Understand the purpose and role of assessment in improving learning outcomes, including the different levels of assessment and the responsibilities of actors involved.
Correctly administer and use the Numeracy Screener Tool, including:
grouping learners and developing remediation plans.
Understand the mandates and complementary roles of SQAD and PMED in monitoring and improving education quality.
Understand the Fidelity of Implementation (FOI) monitoring process, including its sequence and stakeholder roles and responsibilities during monitoring visits.

Initiate, establish, and actively engage in Professional Learning Communities (PLCs) as a mechanism for reflective practice, collaborative professional growth, whole-school development, and improved teaching and learning outcomes.

Use PLC tools, templates, and collaborative problem-solving strategies to analyze classroom challenges, develop inclusive solutions, and create action plans that support learners’ numeracy development.
At the end of the training, the trainers/teachers will be able to:
describe learning gaps the Gambia numeracy curriculum (Goal 1)

explain the importance of the Competency-based Curriculum Framework (CBC) and suggest ways that teachers can make the development of the cross-curricula competencies and socio-emotional skills a priority in implementing the NLNC. (Goal 2)

explain the basic characteristics of a Professional Learning Community (PLC) and their potential for creating a new teaching culture where teachers will be willing to support each other in school (Goal 3).
explain the roles and responsibilities of the key actors in the PLC (REDs/CMs, HTs, DHT/SMs, Coaches and teachers) in your school (Goal 3).
describe the changes in the curriculum introduced with the Gambian numeracy curriculum (GNC) (Goal 4)
use the Teacher Guide and Pupil Book to prepare and demonstrate how to teach a lesson to peers (Goal 5)
describe and demonstrate the teaching concepts: inclusive pedagogies, creative learner-centred pedagogies through demonstration lessons (Goal 6)

describe and demonstrate the assessment concepts: assessment for learning (AFL), assessment of learning (AOL) and assessment as learning (AAL) strategies through demonstrations, using essential tools for assessment, monitoring and reporting on learners’ progress (Goal 6)

Identify barriers that are likely to inhibit the learning of numeracy in the early years; and explain how the barriers related to cross-curricula competencies and socio-emotional skills can be addressed in numeracy lessons (Goal 7)

prepare to teach peers focusing on developing the essential numeracy teaching skills like encouraging math talk, and math reasoning; supporting student explanation and/or justification; recognizing and validating/integrating students’ informal thinking; and creating enabling classroom learning environment. (Goal 7)

By the end of the session participants should be able:

Curriculum should respond to evidence about what learners are actually learning.
The numeracy curriculum was reviewed because assessment evidence showed that many learners were not mastering expected foundational skills.

The session material notes persistent underachievement in foundational numeracy and reports that the 2023 Grade 3 NAT results showed learners mastering only about 40% of literacy and numeracy content taught.
What numeracy challenges do you commonly see among learners?
The curriculum review therefore places stronger emphasis on learner understanding, reasoning, application and foundational numeracy skills.
A Competency-Based Curriculum (CBC) focuses on what learners should know, be able to do, and demonstrate at the end of a learning stage.
Instead of focusing mainly on content coverage, CBC emphasizes:
Determining the knowledge, skills, and attitudes needed.
Planning learning experiences that help learners achieve those competencies.
The focus is not simply on what teachers teach but on what learners can actually do and demonstrate.
The Competency-Based Curriculum uses a Backward Design Approach.
Instead of starting with activities, teachers first identify:
What learners should know and be able to do (competencies).
How they will know learners have achieved those competencies (assessment).
What learning activities will help learners reach the competencies.
Learners can represent the number 8 in different ways.
learner matches 8 objects to the numeral.
What activities could help learners develop this competency?
The activity is chosen because it helps learners achieve the competency, not simply because it is enjoyable or familiar.

blocks.title: Content Focus of the Competency-Based Numeracy Curriculum

content.text: The revised curriculum places greater emphasis on foundational number concepts.
Why is number sense important before learners begin formal calculation?
Learners need to understand quantities and relationships between numbers, not only recite number names or memorize procedures.
Strong foundational understanding supports later mathematical learning.

blocks.title: What Can Be Achieved Through the Competency-Based Numeracy Curriculum?

content.text: Assign each group two competencies from the list below:
Count, subitize, estimate, and verify quantities.
Developmental strategies for addition and subtraction.
Use objects and models to solve problems.
Identify and compare 2D shapes and 3D objects.
What should the learner be able to do?
What evidence would show the learner can do it?
What classroom activity could help develop it?
What is the biggest change a teacher needs to make when moving from content coverage to competency-based teaching?
Competency-based teaching shifts the focus from:
“What can my learners now understand and do?”
The success of the curriculum is therefore measured by what learners can understand, apply, communicate and demonstrate, not simply by how much material has been covered.

sessions.title: Foundational Numeracy Curriculum- Scope and Sequence

content.text: Participants form a circle. The trainer calls out two numbers, and the participant must quickly state their sum.
If the two numbers add up to 5, the correct response is “5.” If the answer is correct, the participant remains in the game.
If the sum is not 5, the participant is eliminated or gives an incorrect response, and another participant takes their turn.

Would you start with the roof before laying the foundation?

Invite 3–4 participants to share their responses.
Learners need strong foundations before moving to more complex concepts.
The curriculum therefore organizes learning through scope, sequence and developmental progression.
Scope refers to the breadth and depth of what learners are expected to learn.
In simple terms, scope answers: What will be taught?
As learners move through the grades, the range of numbers and concepts gradually increases.
Why do you think learners are not introduced to numbers 0–50 immediately in ECD 2?
Allow participants to discuss and share ideas.
The curriculum limits the amount and complexity of content at each level so that learners can develop the necessary foundations first.
Scope and sequence tell us what is taught and when.
Developmental progressions help teachers understand how learners' numerical understanding develops over time.

Recognizing small quantities

This does not mean that every child progresses at exactly the same speed.
The progression helps teachers understand the foundations that support later learning.
Ask participants to work in pairs.

Example 1:
ECD2 works with numbers 0–9, while Grade 1 extends to 0–50.
Is this mainly an example of scope, sequence or developmental progression?

Example 2:
Grade 1 begins with 0–9 and 10 before moving to 11–20 and later 21–50.

Example 3:
A learner develops from counting objects to identifying numerals and representing numbers in different ways.
Why is it important for the teacher to know all three?
Scope helps the teacher know what content belongs at that level.
Sequence helps the teacher know the order.
Developmental progression helps the teacher understand the learning that should develop underneath the content.
How can understanding scope, sequence and developmental progression help you support a learner who is struggling with numeracy?

Effective numeracy teaching requires teachers to know what learners should learn, the order in which learning should develop, and the foundational understanding learners need before moving to more complex concepts.

At the Concrete stage, learners use real objects or manipulatives to explore the mathematical idea.

At the Pictorial stage, learners represent the objects using pictures, drawings or visual models.

At the Abstract stage, learners use numbers and mathematical symbols.

sessions.title: The "I Do, We Do, You Do" Teaching Strategy

content.text: A pair of numbers adding up to 10
Players use number cards from 0 to 10 and work together to find two numbers that add up to 10.
Two participants sit facing each other.
Place the number cards face down on a table.
Player 1 picks a card and says the number aloud.
Player 2 must quickly say the number that makes the total equal to 10.
If the answer is correct, the pair earns 1 point.
Players switch roles after each turn.
Continue until all cards have been used or for a set time
By the end of this session participants should be able to:
Explain the purpose of the “I Do, We Do, You Do” strategy.
Describe the teacher and learner roles at each stage.
Demonstrate how the strategy can be used to teach one foundational numeracy skill.
Think about learning a new skill, such as cooking something new, using a mobile application or riding a bicycle.
Did somebody simply explain it and then leave you to do it independently?
Or did you first see it demonstrated and practise with some support?
Ask participants to discuss with a partner for 1 minute.
Learning often becomes easier when we:
This is the foundation of I Do, We Do, You Do.

blocks.title: What is the "I Do, We Do, You Do" Strategy?

content.text: The "I Do, We Do, You Do" strategy is a gradual release model of instruction.
The strategy ensures learners move from supported learning to independent mastery.

blocks.title: One Skill Through All Three Stages

content.text: Display a collection of four objects.
“Watch me. I will count each object once.”
During I Do, I demonstrate clearly while learners watch and listen.
I can also think aloud so learners understand the process.
The original material describes the teacher as explaining, modelling and thinking aloud during this stage.
During We Do, learners participate, but the teacher is still providing guidance.
The teacher watches responses and provides support or correction when necessary.
The source identifies monitoring, immediate correction and confidence-building as important functions of guided practice.

The teacher observes and provides support only when necessary.

blocks.title: When Should the Teacher Move On?

content.text: What should a teacher do if many learners struggle during the “We Do” stage?
“I Do, We Do, You Do” should not be treated as a rigid timetable.
Teachers should respond to evidence of learner understanding.
This is one of the most important practical messages for teachers.

This is the central idea of the strategy and aligns with the source's emphasis on modelling, guided practice and independent application.

blocks.title: What Does Good Number Sense Look Like?

content.text: Number sense is more than being able to recite numbers.
Learners need to understand how many, connect quantities to numerals, recognize small quantities, and understand relationships between numbers.

blocks.title: Counting: Count to Tell How Many

content.text: Learners need regular opportunities to count real objects.
Counting should help them determine how many objects are in a collection.
Give each pair a small set of bottle tops or counters.

The arrangement changed, but the number of objects remained the same.
Encourage learners to touch or move each object as they count so that each object is counted once.

Sometimes learners should recognise small quantities without counting every object.

Subitizing means recognising a small quantity quickly without counting each object.
It contributes to number sense and helps learners become more flexible with quantities.

Counting = determining how many by counting objects.
Subitizing = recognising how many without counting each object.
Learners also need to understand that a written numeral represents a quantity.

Numeracy lessons in the Teacher Guide are organised into four connected phases:
Mental Math → Reinforcement → New Learning → Closure
Each phase has a specific purpose and contributes to the overall lesson.
Mental Math prepares learners for learning and develops fluency with previously encountered mathematical ideas.
These activities should be quick and lively.

“Show me 5 fingers.”
“What is 1 more than 5?”
“What is 1 less than 5?”
The guide identifies Mental Math activities as M1, M2, M3 and so on, and notes that they should be short and fast-paced.
It helps learners consolidate prior learning before moving forward.

The guide states that reinforcement activities review previously taught concepts and are labelled R1, R2, R3 and so on.
New Learning is the main teaching and learning phase.
It focuses on the lesson’s specific learning outcomes.
During this phase, teachers should use appropriate resources and provide opportunities for active learner participation, discussion and practical learning.

content.text: What are errors and misconceptions in numeracy?
Not all learners’ mistakes mean the same thing.
Some are simple errors, while others reveal misconceptions.
Errors: Occur due to a momentary lapse in attention, misaligned digits during calculations, or reverse counting. These are often non-recurring and easily self-corrected by the learner.
Misconceptions: Deep-seated, systematic errors where the child consistently applies an incorrect rule or overgeneralizes a mathematical concept.
Incorrect ideas that learners consistently apply.
The equal sign means "write the answer."
Bigger numbers always represent bigger quantities.
Why is it important to know the difference?
Adding positive numbers makes it bigger. Adding zero keeps it constant or the same. Adding a negative number makes it smaller.
